name: Channel Kurtosis Analysis
description: Measures excess kurtosis per color channel — AI-generated images often exhibit non-Gaussian channel distributions. Kurtosis, the fourth standardized moment, reveals how a distribution's tails differ from a Gaussian, exposing the unnatural value distributions produced by neural network output layers.
algorithm: Per-Channel Excess Kurtosis + Inter-Channel Ratio Test
mechanism:
Kurtosis is the fourth standardized moment of a distribution, measuring the 'tailedness' relative to a Gaussian: κ = E[(X-μ)⁴]/σ⁴ - 3 (excess kurtosis, where 0 = Gaussian). This detector computes excess kurtosis independently for each color channel (R, G, B) and optionally in transformed color spaces (YCbCr, Lab).

In natural photographs, color channel distributions are shaped by physical light transport: sensor noise contributes Gaussian (κ≈0) components, while scene content creates heavy-tailed distributions (positive kurtosis, typically κ = 1-5). The key forensic signals are: (1) **Per-channel kurtosis values** — AI generators often produce channels with abnormally low kurtosis (sub-Gaussian, κ < 0) because their output layers use sigmoid/tanh activations that compress the distribution tails. (2) **Inter-channel kurtosis ratios** — in real images, the Green channel typically has higher kurtosis than R and B due to Bayer CFA sampling (2 green pixels per 4-pixel block); AI images violate this G>R≈B ordering. (3) **Local kurtosis maps** — computing kurtosis in sliding windows reveals regions where the statistical signature changes abruptly, indicating splicing or inpainting.

The detector outputs an anomaly score based on the deviation of the observed kurtosis vector from expected natural image statistics.
parameters:
Color channels: R, G, B (linear), Y, Cb, Cr
Excess kurtosis formula: κ = μ₄/σ⁴ - 3
Local window size: 32×32 pixels (sliding, stride 16)
Expected natural range: κ ∈ [0.5, 6.0] per channel
Inter-channel ratio test: G-kurtosis > mean(R,B)-kurtosis
Anomaly threshold: Mahalanobis distance from natural centroid
accuracy: Low to Moderate — 60-72% standalone accuracy. Most effective as a fast screening filter; kurtosis alone is insufficient for definitive classification.
source: Lyu, S. & Farid, H. (2005). How Realistic is Photorealistic? IEEE TSP.
useCase: Fast statistical screening of suspected AI-generated images, identifying images with unnaturally uniform channel distributions, detecting inpainting or splicing through local kurtosis discontinuities, and pre-filtering images for deeper forensic analysis.
strengths:
• Extremely fast computation — single-pass histogram statistics per channel
• The inter-channel kurtosis ratio provides a physics-grounded forensic test unique to Bayer-sensor cameras
• Local kurtosis maps can spatially localize manipulated regions
• Works independently of semantic content — purely statistical
limitations:
• Low standalone accuracy — kurtosis is a coarse statistical measure easily influenced by scene content
• Images dominated by flat regions (sky, walls) naturally have low kurtosis regardless of authenticity
• Modern generators with noise injection in output layers can match natural kurtosis ranges
• Heavy post-processing (gamma correction, levels) dramatically alters channel kurtosis

references.title: Lyu, S. & Farid, H. (2005). How Realistic is Photorealistic? IEEE TSP.
Ng, T.T. et al. (2004). Using Geometry Invariants for Camera Response Function Estimation. CVPR.
